content: This document is designed to provide information in an adapted format to assist women, girls, and their families in making informed decisions regarding cervical cancer screening and treatment. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends two primary strategies for cervical cancer prevention in the general population of women. The first strategy involves the use of HPV DNA detection in a screen-and-treat approach, starting at the age of 30, with regular screening intervals of every 5 to 10 years. For women living with HIV, the WHO suggests a different approach: HPV DNA detection in a screen, triage, and treat strategy, beginning at the age of 25, with regular screening every 3 to 5 years. The WHO guidelines emphasize the right of all individuals to equality and non-discrimination in accessing sexual and reproductive health care. While most evidence on cervical cancer is derived from studies involving cisgender women, the guidelines acknowledge that transgender men, non-binary individuals, gender-fluid individuals, and intersex individuals with a female reproductive system also require cervical cancer prevention services. For simplicity and readability, the term women is used inclusively to refer to all gender-diverse individuals at risk for cervical cancer. The updated guidelines were developed following the methods outlined in the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development, second edition. The process included contributions from various groups, including the Guideline Development Group (GDG), External Review Group (ERG), systematic review teams, and modeling teams. The WHO Secretariat, comprising staff from relevant WHO departments and the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), coordinated the guideline development process. The GDG consisted of 53 members (35 women and 18 men) from all six WHO regions, including representatives from civil society organizations, women's groups, and women living with HIV. These members brought diverse expertise in cervical screening and treatment. Two members served as co-chairs to moderate GDG meetings. An ERG, composed of 18 members with expertise in research, policy development, program implementation, and clinical care, provided peer review for the guideline document. Evidence relevant to HPV mRNA testing was synthesized through systematic reviews, mathematical modeling, and surveys. Two teams conducted evidence reviews on the accuracy of HPV mRNA versus HPV DNA detection for identifying CIN2+ and CIN3+ lesions, as well as longitudinal evidence on HPV mRNA test use. Another team developed a mathematical model to evaluate HPV mRNA testing in the general population of women. The Policy1-Cervix platform, a validated dynamic model of HPV transmission, vaccination, and cervical cancer outcomes, was used to predict outcomes in women across 78 lowand middle-income countries. The GDG also considered values, preferences, feasibility, acceptability, resource use, and equity in developing recommendations. Surveys and systematic reviews were conducted to gather input from women, healthcare providers, and other stakeholders. The evidence was assessed using the GRADE methodology and presented in evidence-to-decision (EtD) tables to facilitate decision-making. The GDG meetings, held virtually, focused on formulating recommendations. Consensus was reached on all recommendations, which were then electronically approved by GDG members. Strong recommendations, indicated by the phrase WHO recommends, were made when the benefits of an intervention clearly outweighed the harms.
